texts: bad: 'day 0 of Year 1' is forced onto the calendar day-of-month term as (Day 0), a date that does not exist - an epoch-relative day index has no term of its own - and 'the night of the autumn equinox' gets only an opaque association link, so nothing actually dates the night to the equinox. Date the night by the equinox and keep the year: 'In Year 1, the night of the autumn equinox was clear and mild.' If the day index has to survive, give it as a real month and day, since 'day N of Year N' has no carrier.

bad: 'about twenty-five' cannot be carried at all - a count has to be a plain integer, and hedging it pushed a distribution into the count slot, so the number is either ill-typed (as here) or dropped outright; and 'at each lantern' turns the whole clause into a standing per-lantern rule, so nothing in the parse says a counting actually happened that night. Drop the hedge and count one named set: 'Keepers counted twenty-five nightmoths at the lanterns of the Cliff Path.' If the per-lantern figure is the point, keep the universal but use an exact numeral - 'Keepers counted twenty-five nightmoths at each lantern of the Cliff Path' - and expect a per-lantern rule rather than a recorded count.
good. 'a crowd of nightmoths' yields both the crowd witness and its nightmoth membership, and the gathering is correctly one collective event located at the East Row.
good. the three sky-cats become a counted group with a descent event from the spires, plus a per-member rule so each cat's own descent is derivable; both compounds get their genus links.
good. reuses the same sky-cat group and the same nightmoth crowd introduced earlier, with the East Row correctly attached as the hunt's location.

bad: two losses here - 'shrank' put the crowd in the role reserved for a participant that does NOT change, understating that the crowd got smaller (that one is a translator-side slip, not a wording problem), and the NP-internal 'at the East Row' was dropped entirely, so the shrinking is unlocated. Fronting the locative attaches it to the event, where it survives: 'At the East Row, the nightmoth crowd shrank.'

mixed: the sentence itself parses faithfully - keepers, seven nightmoths, the East Row and the third watch are all recorded - but 'seven nightmoths' mints a fresh set with no link to the crowd that shrank, so the passage never records that the crowd fell to seven. Tie the count to the crowd with a partitive: 'Keepers counted seven of the nightmoth crowd at the East Row at the third watch.'
good. parses as a fireable rule - each nightmoth that survived the hunt gets its own flight to the Hollows - keyed to the hunt event that sentence 5 asserts at top level.
